entries.1066c3b77af0b5893a05cb9e4c50d7aec81cc4d0: <div sID="gen15768" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="13" osisID="Isa.13" sID="Isa.13"/> <div eID="gen15768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15769" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15770" type="x-p"/> Hitherto the prophecies of this book related only to Judah and Israel, and Jerusalem especially; but now the prophet begins to look abroad, and to read the doom of divers of the neighbouring states and kingdoms: for he that is King of saints is also King of nations, and rules in the affairs of the children of men as well as in those of his own children. But the nations to whom these prophecies do relate were all such as the people of God were in some way or other conversant and concerned with, such as had been kind or unkind to Israel, and accordingly God would deal with them, either in favour or in wrath; for the Lord's portion is his people, and to them he has an eye in all the dispensations of his providence concerning those about them, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.8-Deut.32.9">Deut. xxxii. 8, 9</reference>. The threatenings we find here against Babylon, Moab, Damascus, Egypt, Tyre, &c., were intended for comfort to those in Israel that feared God, but were terrified and oppressed by those potent neighbours, and for alarm to those among them that were wicked. If God would thus severely reckon with those for their sins that knew him not, and made no profession of his name, how severe would he be with those that were called by his name and yet lived in rebellion against him! And perhaps the directing of particular prophecies to the neighbouring nations might invite some of those nations to the reading of the Jews' Bible, and so they might be brought to their religion. This chapter, and that which follows, contain what God had to say to Babylon and Babylon's king, who were at present little known to Israel, but would in process of time become a greater enemy to them than any other had been, for which God would at last reckon with them. In this chapter we have, I. A general rendezvous of the forces that were to be employed against Babylon, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.1-Isa.13.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. The dreadfully bloody work that those forces should make in Babylon, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.6-Isa.13.18">ver. 6-18</reference>. III. The utter ruin and desolation of Babylon, which this should end in, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.19-Isa.13.22">ver. 19-22</reference>.
entries.e822ffe07e64a1650725ce01b47bf2e31c4b3919: <div eID="gen15770" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15769" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Doom of Babylon. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 739.)</title> <div sID="gen15771" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amoz did see. <hi type="super">2</hi> Lift ye up a banner upon the high mountain, exalt the voice unto them, shake the hand, that they may go into the gates of the nobles. <hi type="super">3</hi> I have commanded my sanctified ones, I have also called my mighty ones for mine anger, <hi type="italic">even</hi> them that rejoice in my highness. <hi type="super">4</hi> The noise of a multitude in the mountains, like as of a great people; a tumultuous noise of the kingdoms of nations gathered together: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts mustereth the host of the battle. <hi type="super">5</hi> They come from a far country, from the end of heaven, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and the weapons of his indignation, to destroy the whole land. <div eID="gen15771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15772" type="x-p"/> The general title of this book was, <hi type="italic">The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.1">ch. i. 1</reference>. Here we have that which Isaiah saw, which was represented to his mind as clearly and fully as if he had seen it with his bodily eyes; but the particular inscription of this sermon is <hi type="italic">the burden of Babylon.</hi> 1. It is a burden, a lesson they were to learn (so some understand it), but they would be loth to learn it, and it would be a burden to their memories, or a load which should lie heavily upon them and under which they should sink. Those that will not make the word of God their rest (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.12">ch. xxviii. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.16">Jer. vi. 16</reference>) shall find it made a burden to them. 2. It is the burden of Babylon or Babel, which at this time was a dependent upon the Assyrian monarchy (the metropolis of which was Nineveh), but soon after revolted from it and became a monarchy of itself, and a very potent one, in Nebuchadnezzar. This prophet afterwards foretold the captivity of the Jews in Babylon, <reference osisRef="Isa.39.6">ch. xxxix. 6</reference>. Here he foretels the reprisals God would make upon Babylon for the wrongs done to his people. In these verses a summons is given to those powerful and warlike nations whom God would make us of as the instruments of his wrath for the destruction of Babylon: he afterwards names them (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.17">v. 17</reference>) the <hi type="italic">Medes,</hi> who, in conjunction with the Persians, under the command of Darius and Cyrus, were the ruin of the Babylonian monarchy. <div eID="gen15772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15773" type="x-p"/> I. The place doomed to destruction is Babylon; it is here called <hi type="italic">the gates of the nobles</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.2">v. 2</reference>), because of the abundance of noblemen's houses that were in it, stately ones and richly furnished, which would invite the enemy to come, in hopes of a rich booty. The gates of nobles were strong and well guarded, and yet they would be no fence against those who came with commission to execute God's judgments. Before his power and wrath palaces are no more than cottages. Nor is it only the gates of the nobles, but <hi type="italic">the whole land,</hi> that is doomed to destruction (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.5">v. 5</reference>); for, though the nobles were the leaders in persecuting and oppressing God's people, yet the whole land concurred with them in it. <div eID="gen15773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15774" type="x-p"/> II. The persons brought together to lay Babylon waste are here called, 1. God's <hi type="italic">sanctified ones</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.3">v. 3</reference>), designed for this service and set apart to it by the purpose and providence of God, disengaged from other projects, that they might wholly apply themselves to this, such as were qualified for that to which they were called, for what work God employs men in he does in some measure fit them for. It intimates likewise that in God's intention, though not in theirs, it was a holy war; they designed only the enlargement of their own empire, but God designed the release of his people and a type of the destruction of the New-Testament Babylon. Cyrus, the person principally concerned, was justly called <hi type="italic">a sanctified one,</hi> for he was God's anointed (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.1">ch. xlv. 1</reference>) and a figure of him that was to come. It is a pity but all soldiers, especially those that fight the Lord's battles, should be in the strictest sense sanctified ones; and it is a wonder that those dare be profane ones who carry their lives in their hands. 2. They are called God's <hi type="italic">mighty ones,</hi> because they had their might from God and were now to use it for him. It is said of Cyrus that in this expedition <hi type="italic">God held his right hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.45.1">ch. xlv. 1</reference>. God's sanctified ones are his mighty ones. Those whom God calls he qualifies; and those whom he makes holy he makes strong in spirit. 3. They are said to rejoice in his highness, that is, to serve his glory and the purposes of it with great alacrity. Though Cyrus did not know God, nor actually design his honour in what he did, yet God used him as his servant (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.4">ch. xlv. 4</reference>, <hi type="italic">I have surnamed thee</hi> as my servant, though <hi type="italic">thou hast not known me</hi>), and he rejoiced in those successes by which God exalted his own name. 4. They are very numerous, <hi type="italic">a multitude, a great people, kingdoms of nations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.4">v. 4</reference>), not rude and barbarous, but modelled and regular troops, such as are furnished out by well-ordered kingdoms. The great God has hosts at his command. 5. They are far-fetched: <hi type="italic">They come from a far country, from the end of</hi> heaven. The vast country of Assyria lay between Babylon and Persia. God can make those a scourge and ruin to his enemies that lie most remote from them and therefore are least dreaded. <div eID="gen15774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15775" type="x-p"/> III. The summons given them is effectual, their obedience ready, and they make a very formidable appearance: <hi type="italic">A banner is lifted up upon the high mountain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.13.2">v. 2</reference>. God's standard is set up, a flag of defiance hung out against Babylon. It is erected on high, where all may see it; whoever will may come and enlist themselves under it, and they shall be taken immediately into God's pay. Those that beat up for volunteers must <hi type="italic">exalt the voice</hi> in making proclamation, to encourage soldiers to come in; they must <hi type="italic">shake the hand,</hi> to beckon those at a distance and to animate those that have enlisted themselves. And they shall not do this in vain; God has commanded and called those whom he designs to make use of (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.3">v. 3</reference>) and power goes along with his calls and commands, which cannot be resisted. He that makes men able to serve him can, when he pleases, make them willing too. It is the <hi type="italic">Lord of hosts that musters the host of the battle,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.13.4">v. 4</reference>. He raises them, brings them together, puts them in order, reviews them, has an exact account of them in his muster-roll, sees that they be all in their respective posts, and gives them their necessary orders. Note, All the hosts of war are under the command of the Lord of hosts; and that which makes them truly formidable is that, when they come against Babylon, the Lord comes, and brings them with him as <hi type="italic">the weapons of his indignation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.13.5">v. 5</reference>. Note, Great princes and armies are but tools in God's hand, weapons that he is pleased to make use of in doing his work, and it is his wrath that arms them and gives them success.
entries.4c3f19d258685c718a10b6929fc990ed1d7cdf30: <div eID="gen15775" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Doom of Babylon. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 739.)</title> <div sID="gen15776" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Howl ye; for the day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> at hand; it shall come as a destruction from the Almighty. <hi type="super">7</hi> Therefore shall all hands be faint, and every man's heart shall melt: <hi type="super">8</hi> And they shall be afraid: pangs and sorrows shall take hold of them; they shall be in pain as a woman that travaileth: they shall be amazed one at another; their faces <hi type="italic">shall be as</hi> flames. <hi type="super">9</hi> Behold, the day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> cometh, cruel both with wrath and fierce anger, to lay the land desolate: and he shall destroy the sinners thereof out of it. <hi type="super">10</hi> For the stars of heaven and the constellations thereof shall not give their light: the sun shall be darkened in his going forth, and the moon shall not cause her light to shine. <hi type="super">11</hi> And I will punish the world for <hi type="italic">their</hi> evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; and I will cause the arrogancy of the proud to cease, and will lay low the haughtiness of the terrible. <hi type="super">12</hi> I will make a man more precious than fine gold; even a man than the golden wedge of Ophir. <hi type="super">13</hi> Therefore I will shake the heavens, and the earth shall remove out of her place, in the wrath of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, and in the day of his fierce anger. <hi type="super">14</hi> And it shall be as the chased roe, and as a sheep that no man taketh up: they shall every man turn to his own people, and flee every one into his own land. <hi type="super">15</hi> Every one that is found shall be thrust through; and every one that is joined <hi type="italic">unto them</hi> shall fall by the sword. <hi type="super">16</hi> Their children also shall be dashed to pieces before their eyes; their houses shall be spoiled, and their wives ravished. <hi type="super">17</hi> Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, which shall not regard silver; and <hi type="italic">as for</hi> gold, they shall not delight in it. <hi type="super">18</hi> <hi type="italic">Their</hi> bows also shall dash the young men to pieces; and they shall have no pity on the fruit of the womb; their eye shall not spare children. <div eID="gen15776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15777" type="x-p"/> We have here a very elegant and lively description of the terrible confusion and desolation which should be made in Babylon by the descent which the Medes and Persians should make upon it. Those that were now secure and easy were bidden to <hi type="italic">howl</hi> and make sad lamentation; for, <div eID="gen15777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15778" type="x-p"/> I. God was about to appear in wrath against them, and it is a fearful thing to fall into his hands: <hi type="italic">The day of the Lord is at hand</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.6">v. 6</reference>), a little day of judgment, when God will act as a just avenger of his own and his people's injured cause. And there are those who will have reason to tremble when that day is at hand. <hi type="italic">The day of the Lord cometh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.13.9">v. 9</reference>. Men have their day now, and they think to carry the day; but God laughs at them, for he sees that <hi type="italic">his day is coming,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.37.13">Ps. xxxvii. 13</reference>. Fury is not with God, and yet his day of reckoning with the Babylonians is said to be <hi type="italic">cruel with wrath and fierce anger.</hi> God will deal in severity with them for the severities they exercised upon God's people; with the froward, with the cruel, he will show himself froward, will show himself cruel, and give the blood-thirsty blood to drink. <div eID="gen15778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15779" type="x-p"/> II. Their hearts shall fail them, and they shall have neither courage nor comfort left; they shall not be able either to resist the judgment coming or to bear up under it, either to oppose the enemy or to support themselves, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.7-Isa.13.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. Those that in the day of their peace were <hi type="italic">proud,</hi> and <hi type="italic">haughty,</hi> and <hi type="italic">terrible</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.11">v. 11</reference>), shall, when trouble comes, be quite dispirited and at their wits' end: <hi type="italic">All hands shall be faint,</hi> and unable to hold a weapon, <hi type="italic">and every man's heart shall melt,</hi> so that they shall be ready to die for fear. The pangs of their fear shall be like those of a woman in hard labour, and <hi type="italic">they shall be amazed one at another.</hi> In frightening themselves, they shall frighten one another; they shall wonder to see those tremble that used to be bold and daring; or they shall be amazed looking one at another, as men at a loss, <reference osisRef="Gen.42.1">Gen. xlii. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Their faces shall be as flames,</hi> pale as flames, through fear (so some), or red as flames sometimes are, blushing at their own cowardice; or their faces shall be as faces scorched with the flame, or as theirs that labour in the fire, their <hi type="italic">visage blacker than a coal,</hi> or like <hi type="italic">a bottle in the smoke,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.83">Ps. cxix. 83</reference>. <div eID="gen15779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15780" type="x-p"/> III. All comfort and hope shall fail them (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">The stars of heaven shall not give their light,</hi> but shall be clouded and overcast; <hi type="italic">the sun shall be darkened in his going forth,</hi> rising bright, but lost again, a certain sign of foul weather. They shall be as men in distress at sea, when neither sun nor stars appear, <reference osisRef="Acts.27.20">Acts xxvii. 20</reference>. It shall be as dreadful a time with them as it would be with the earth if all the heavenly luminaries were turned into darkness, a resemblance of the day of judgment, when the sun shall be turned into darkness. The heavens frowning thus is an indication of the displeasure of the God of heaven. When things look dark on earth, yet it is well enough if all be clear upwards; but, if we have no comfort thence, wherewith shall we be comforted? <div eID="gen15780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15781" type="x-p"/> IV. God will visit them <hi type="italic">for their iniquity;</hi> and all this is intended for the punishment of sin, and particularly the sin of pride, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.11">v. 11</reference>. This puts wormwood and gall into the affliction and misery, 1. That sin must now have its punishment. Though Babylon be a little world, yet, being a wicked world, it shall not go unpunished. Sin brings desolation on the world of the ungodly; and when the kingdoms of the earth are quarrelling with one another it is the fruit of God's controversy with them all. 2. That pride must now have its fall: <hi type="italic">The haughtiness of the terrible</hi> must now be <hi type="italic">laid low,</hi> particularly of Nebuchadnezzar and his son Belshazzar, who had, in their pride, trampled upon, and made themselves very terrible to, the people of God. <hi type="italic">A man's pride will bring him low.</hi> <div eID="gen15781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15782" type="x-p"/> V. There shall be so great a slaughter as will produce a scarcity of men (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will make a man more precious than fine gold.</hi> You could not have a man to be employed in any of the affairs of state, not a man to be enlisted in the army, not a man to match a daughter to, for the building up of a family, if you would give any money for one. The troops of the neighbouring nations would not be hired into the service of the king of Babylon, because they saw every thing go against him. Populous countries are soon depopulated by war. And God can soon make a kingdom that has been courted and admired to be dreaded and shunned by all, as a house that is falling, or a ship that is sinking. <div eID="gen15782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15783" type="x-p"/> VI. There shall be a universal confusion and consternation, such a confusion of their affairs that it shall be like the <hi type="italic">shaking of the heavens</hi> with dreadful thunders and the <hi type="italic">removing of the earth</hi> by no less dreadful earthquakes. All shall go to rack and ruin <hi type="italic">in the day of the wrath of the Lord of hosts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.13.13">v. 13</reference>. And such a consternation shall seize their spirits that Babylon, which used to be like a roaring lion and a raging bear to all about her, shall become <hi type="italic">as a chased roe and as a sheep that no man takes up,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.13.14">v. 14</reference>. The army they shall bring into the field, consisting of troops of divers nations (as great armies usually do), shall be so dispirited by their own apprehensions and so dispersed by their enemies' sword that they shall <hi type="italic">turn every man to his own people;</hi> each man shall shift for his own safety; the <hi type="italic">men of might shall not find their hands</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.5">Ps. lxxvi. 5</reference>), but take to their heels. <div eID="gen15783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15784" type="x-p"/> VII. There shall be a general scene of blood and horror, as is usual where the sword devours. No wonder that every one makes the best of his way, since the conqueror gives no quarter, but puts all to the sword, and not those only that are found in arms, as is usual with us even in the most cruel slaughters (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Every one that is found alive shall be run through,</hi> as soon as ever it appears that he is a Babylonian. Nay, because the sword devours one as well as another, <hi type="italic">every one that is joined to them shall fall by the sword;</hi> those of other nations that come in to their assistance shall be cut off with them. It is dangerous being in bad company, and helping those whom God is about to destroy. Those particularly that join themselves to Babylon must expect to share in her plagues, <reference osisRef="Rev.18.4">Rev. xviii. 4</reference>. And, since the most sacred laws of nature, and of humanity itself, are silenced by the fury of war (though they cannot be cancelled), the conquerors shall, in the most barbarous brutish manner, <hi type="italic">dash the children to pieces, and ravish the wives. Jusque datum sceleri—Wickedness shall have free course,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.13.16">v. 16</reference>. They had thus dealt with God's people (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.11">Lam. v. 11</reference>), and now they shall be paid in their own coin, <reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">Rev. xiii. 10</reference>. It was particularly foretold (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.9">Ps. cxxxvii. 9</reference>) that the <hi type="italic">little ones of Babylon should be dashed against the stones.</hi> How cruel soever and unjust those were that did it, God was righteous who suffered it to be done, and to be done <hi type="italic">before their eyes,</hi> to their greater terror and vexation. It was just also that the houses which they had filled with the spoil of Israel should be spoiled and plundered. What is got by rapine is often lost in the same manner. <div eID="gen15784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15785" type="x-p"/> VIII. The enemy that God will send against them shall be inexorable, probably being by some provocation or other more than ordinarily exasperated against them; or, in whatever way it may be brought about, God himself will <hi type="italic">stir up the Medes</hi> to use this severity with the Babylonians. He will not only serve his own purposes by their dispositions and designs, but will put it into their hearts to make this attempt upon Babylon, and suffer them to prosecute it with all this fury. God is not the author of sin, but he would not permit it if he did not know how to bring glory to himself out of it. These Medes, in conjunction with the Persians, shall make thorough work of it; for, 1. They shall take no bribes, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.17">v. 17</reference>. All that men have they would give for their lives, but the Medes <hi type="italic">shall not regard silver;</hi> it is blood they thirst for, not gold; no man's riches shall with them be the ransom of his life. 2. They shall show no pity (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.18">v. 18</reference>), not to <hi type="italic">the young men</hi> that are in the prime of their time—they shall shoot them through with their bows, and then <hi type="italic">dash them to pieces;</hi> not to the age of innocency—<hi type="italic">they shall have no pity on the fruit of the womb, nor spare little children,</hi> whose cries and frights one would think should make even marble eyes to weep, and hearts of adamant to relent. Pause a little here and wonder, (1.) That men should be thus cruel and inhuman, and so utterly divested of all compassion; and in it see how corrupt and degenerate the nature of man has become. (2.) That the God of infinite mercy should suffer it, nay, and should make it to be the execution of his justice, which shows that, though he is gracious, yet he is the God to whom vengeance belongs. (3.) That little infants, who have never been guilty of any actual sin, should be thus abused, which shows that there is an original guilt by which life is forfeited as soon as it is had.
entries.f3e133c679a7bc097cb10e6ccc4359027c674859: <div eID="gen15785" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Doom of Babylon. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 739.)</title> <div sID="gen15786" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the beauty of the Chaldees' excellency, shall be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. <hi type="super">20</hi> It shall never be inhabited, neither shall it be dwelt in from generation to generation: neither shall the Arabian pitch tent there; neither shall the shepherds make their fold there. <hi type="super">21</hi> But wild beasts of the desert shall lie there; and their houses shall be full of doleful creatures; and owls shall dwell there, and satyrs shall dance there. <hi type="super">22</hi> And the wild beasts of the islands shall cry in their desolate houses, and dragons in <hi type="italic">their</hi> pleasant palaces: and her time <hi type="italic">is</hi> near to come, and her days shall not be prolonged. <div eID="gen15786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15787" type="x-p"/> The great havoc and destruction which it was foretold should be made by the Medes and Persians in Babylon here end in the final destruction of it. 1. It is allowed that Babylon was a noble city. It was <hi type="italic">the glory of kingdoms and the beauty of the Chaldees' excellency;</hi> it was that <hi type="italic">head of gold</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.37-Dan.2.38">Dan. ii. 37, 38</reference>); it was called <hi type="italic">the lady of kingdoms</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.5">ch. xlvii. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">the praise of the whole earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.41">Jer. li. 41</reference>), <hi type="italic">like a pleasant roe</hi> (so the word signifies); but it shall be as a <hi type="italic">chased roe,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.13.14">v. 14</reference>. The Chaldeans gloried in the beauty and wealth of this their metropolis. 2. It is foretold that it should be wholly destroyed, like Sodom and Gomorrah; not so miraculously, nor so suddenly, but as effectually, though gradually; and the destruction should come upon them as that upon Sodom, when they were secure, eating and drinking, <reference osisRef="Luke.17.28-Luke.17.29">Luke xvii. 28, 29</reference>. Babylon was taken when Belshazzar was in his revels; and, though Cyrus and Darius did not demolish it, yet by degrees it wasted away and in process of time it went all to ruin. It is foretold here (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.20">v. 20</reference>) <hi type="italic">that it shall never be inhabited;</hi> in Adrian's time nothing remained but the wall. And whereas it is prophesied concerning Nineveh, that great city, that when it should be deserted and left desolate yet flocks should lie down in the midst of it, it is here said concerning Babylon that <hi type="italic">the Arabians,</hi> who were <hi type="italic">shepherds, should not make their folds there;</hi> the country about should be so barren that there would be no grazing there; no, not for sheep. Nay, it shall be the receptacle of <hi type="italic">wild beasts,</hi> that affect solitude; the houses of Babylon, where the sons and daughters of pleasure used to rendezvous, <hi type="italic">shall be full of doleful creatures, owls and satyrs,</hi> that are themselves frightened thither, as to a place proper for them, and by whom all others are frightened thence. Historians say that this was fulfilled in the letter. Benjamin Bar-Jona, in his Itinerary, speaking of Babel, has these words: "This is that Babel which was of old thirty miles in breadth; it is now laid waste. There are yet to be seen the ruins of a palace of Nebuchadnezzar, but the sons of men dare not enter in, for fear of serpents and scorpions, which possess the place." Let none be proud of their pompous palaces, for they know not but they may become worse than cottages; nor let any think that <hi type="italic">their houses shall endure for ever</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.11">Ps. xlix. 11</reference>), when perhaps nothing may remain but the ruins and reproaches of them. 3. It is intimated that this destruction should come shortly (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">Her time is near to come.</hi> This prophecy of the destruction of Babylon was intended for the support and comfort of the people of God when they were captives there and grievously oppressed; and the accomplishment of the prophecy was nearly 200 years after the time when it was delivered; yet it followed soon after the time for which it was calculated. When the people of Israel were groaning under the heavy yoke of Babylonish tyranny, sitting down in tears by the rivers of Babylon and upbraided with the songs of Zion, when their insolent oppressors were most haughty and arrogant (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.11">v. 11</reference>), then let them know, for their comfort, that Babylon's time, her day to fall, is near to come, and the days of her prosperity shall not be prolonged, as they have been. When God begins with her he will make an end. Thus it is said of the destruction of the New-Testament Babylon, whereof the former was a type, <hi type="italic">In one hour has her judgment come.</hi>  <chapter eID="Isa.13"/> <div eID="gen15787" type="x-p"/>

entries.99226c07fe73715b41a92a1401aa7c3214eb728e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8548"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 13</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.13.1-Isa.13.22">Is 13:1-22</reference>. The Thirteenth through Twenty-third Chapters Contain Prophecies as to Foreign Nations.--The Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Twenty-seventh Chapters as to Babylon and Assyria.</title> <div sID="gen13951" type="x-p"/> The predictions as to foreign nations are for the sake of the covenant people, to preserve them from despair, or reliance on human confederacies, and to strengthen their faith in God: also in order to extirpate narrow-minded nationality: God is Jehovah to Israel, not for Israel's sake alone, but that He may be thereby Elohim to the nations. These prophecies are in their right chronological place, in the beginning of Hezekiah's reign; then the nations of Western Asia, on the Tigris and Euphrates, first assumed a most menacing aspect.<div eID="gen13951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13952" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8548"/><hi type="bold">1. burden--</hi>weighty or mournful prophecy [Grotius]. Otherwise, simply, the prophetical declaration, from a Hebrew root to put forth with the voice anything, as in <reference osisRef="Num.23.7">Nu 23:7</reference> [Maurer].<div eID="gen13952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13953" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of Babylon--</hi>concerning Babylon. <div eID="gen13953" type="x-p"/>
entries.1b12d37e14be03bf90f6e6afc893d572cdaf0227: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8549"/><div sID="gen13954" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8549"/><hi type="bold">2. Lift ... banner--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.5.26">Is 5:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.10">11:10</reference>).<div eID="gen13954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13955" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the high mountain--</hi>rather, "a bare (literally, "bald," that is, without trees) mountain"; from it the banner could be seen afar off, so as to rally together the peoples against Babylon.<div eID="gen13955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13956" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto them--</hi>unto the Medes (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.17">Is 13:17</reference>), the assailants of Babylon. It is remarkable that Isaiah does not foretell here the Jews' captivity in Babylon, but presupposes that event, and throws himself beyond, predicting another event still more future, the overthrow of the city of Israel's oppressors. It was now one hundred seventy-four years before the event.<div eID="gen13956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13957" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shake ... hand--</hi>beckon with the hand--wave the hand to direct the nations to march against Babylon.<div eID="gen13957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13958" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nobles--</hi>Babylonian. Rather, in a bad sense, tyrants; as in <reference osisRef="Isa.14.5">Is 14:5</reference>, "rulers" in parallelism to "the wicked"; and <reference osisRef="Job.21.28">Job 21:28</reference> [Maurer]. <div eID="gen13958" type="x-p"/>
entries.f2a0f3c921c0ca1a7c59d98f72ab013c8b97d8d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8550"/><div sID="gen13959" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8550"/><hi type="bold">3. sanctified ones--</hi>the Median and Persian soldiers solemnly set apart by Me for the destruction of Babylon, not inwardly "sanctified," but designated to fulfil God's holy purpose (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.27">Jr 51:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.28">28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.3.9">Joe 3:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joel.3.11">11</reference>; where the Hebrew for prepare war is "sanctify" war).<div eID="gen13959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13960" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for mine anger--</hi>to execute it.<div eID="gen13960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13961" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rejoice in my highness--</hi>"Those who are made to triumph for My honor" [Horsley]. The heathen Medes could not be said to "rejoice in God's highness" Maurer translates, "My haughtily exulting ones" (<reference osisRef="Zeph.3.11">Zep 3:11</reference>); a special characteristic of the Persians [Herodotus,1.88]. They rejoiced in their own highness, but it was His that they were unconsciously glorifying. <div eID="gen13961" type="x-p"/>
entries.ad4534f9290eb14f5dd8da7a622d2b9fa61f4526: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8551"/><div sID="gen13962" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8551"/><hi type="bold">4. the mountains--</hi>namely, which separate Media and Assyria, and on one of which the banner to rally the hosts is supposed to be reared.<div eID="gen13962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13963" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tumultuous noise--</hi>The Babylonians are vividly depicted as hearing some unwonted sound like the din of a host; they try to distinguish the sounds, but can only perceive a tumultuous noise.<div eID="gen13963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13964" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nations--</hi>Medes, Persians, and Armenians composed Cyrus' army. <div eID="gen13964" type="x-p"/>
entries.c90fc18a9748a7cbcb1014e8d36153fa398b7cdf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8552"/><div sID="gen13965" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8552"/><hi type="bold">5. They--</hi>namely, "Jehovah," and the armies which are "the weapons of His indignation."<div eID="gen13965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13966" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">far country--</hi>Media and Persia, stretching to the far north and east.<div eID="gen13966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13967" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">end of heaven--</hi>the far east (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.6">Psa 19:6</reference>).<div eID="gen13967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13968" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">destroy--</hi>rather, "to seize" [Horsley]. <div eID="gen13968" type="x-p"/>
entries.19cf0e18dea9d8c61ea13b954a8f341c4aaedb70: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8553"/><div sID="gen13969" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8553"/><hi type="bold">6. day of the Lord--</hi>day of His vengeance on Babylon (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.12">Is 2:12</reference>). Type of the future "day of wrath" (<reference osisRef="Rev.6.17">Re 6:17</reference>).<div eID="gen13969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13970" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">destruction--</hi>literally, "a devastating tempest."<div eID="gen13970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13971" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the Almighty--</hi>not from mere man; therefore irresistible. "Almighty," Hebrew, Shaddai. <div eID="gen13971" type="x-p"/>
entries.dd7004bc8509e191f57a68071a06e7c36c5e98c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8554"/><div sID="gen13972" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8554"/><hi type="bold">7. faint ... melt--</hi>So <reference osisRef="Jer.50.43">Jr 50:43</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Josh.7.5">Jos 7:5</reference>. Babylon was taken by surprise on the night of Belshazzar's impious feast (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.30">Da 5:30</reference>). Hence the sudden fainting and melting of hearts. <div eID="gen13972" type="x-p"/>
entries.173253afee166f52100a46e7d1b93029461763d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8555"/><div sID="gen13973" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8555"/><hi type="bold">8. pangs--</hi>The Hebrew means also a "messenger." Horsley, therefore, with the Septuagint translates, "The heralds (who bring word of the unexpected invasion) are terrified." Maurer agrees with English Version, literally, "they shall take hold of pangs and sorrows."<div eID="gen13973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13974" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">woman ... travaileth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.3">1Th 5:3</reference>).<div eID="gen13974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13975" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">amazed--</hi>the stupid, bewildered gaze of consternation.<div eID="gen13975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13976" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">faces ... flames--</hi>"their visages have the livid hue of flame" [Horsley]; with anguish and indignation. <div eID="gen13976" type="x-p"/>
entries.afc1a4a29cf3cdbc069267f214bf7f1c2cb2e5bf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8556"/><div sID="gen13977" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8556"/><hi type="bold">9. cruel--</hi>not strictly, but unsparingly just; opposed to mercy. Also answering to the cruelty (in the strict sense) of Babylon towards others (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.17">Is 14:17</reference>) now about to be visited on itself.<div eID="gen13977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13978" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the land--</hi>"the earth" [Horsley]. The language of <reference osisRef="Isa.13.9-Isa.13.13">Is 13:9-13</reference> can only primarily and partially apply to Babylon; fully and exhaustively, the judgments to come, hereafter, on the whole earth. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.13.10">Is 13:10</reference> with <reference osisRef="Matt.24.29">Mt 24:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.8.12">Re 8:12</reference>. The sins of Babylon, arrogancy (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.11">Is 13:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.11">Is 14:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.47.7">47:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.8">8</reference>), cruelty, false worship (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.38">Jr 50:38</reference>), persecution of the people of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.6">Is 47:6</reference>), are peculiarly characteristic of the Antichristian world of the latter days (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.32-Dan.11.37">Da 11:32-37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.17.3">Re 17:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.17.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.6">18:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9-Rev.7.14">7, 9-14</reference>, 24). <div eID="gen13978" type="x-p"/>
entries.b4b95798df955ed68f579d74778126782ea9f5ae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8557"/><div sID="gen13979" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8557"/><hi type="bold">10. stars, &c.--</hi>figuratively for anarchy, distress, and revolutions of kingdoms (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.4">Is 34:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.10">Joe 2:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.7">Eze 32:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.8.9">Am 8:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.6.12-Rev.6.14">Re 6:12-14</reference>). There may be a literal fulfilment finally, shadowed forth under this imagery (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.1">Re 21:1</reference>).<div eID="gen13979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">constellations--</hi>Hebrew, "a fool," or "impious one"; applied to the constellation Orion, which was represented as an impious giant (Nimrod deified, the founder of Babylon) chained to the sky. See on <reference osisRef="Job.38.31">Job 38:31</reference>. <div eID="gen13980" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f7a71b1ba2717379c07afcee3d3c4dc470590fa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8558"/><div sID="gen13981" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8558"/><hi type="bold">11. world--</hi>the impious of the world (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Is 11:4</reference>).<div eID="gen13981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13982" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">arrogancy--</hi>Babylon's besetting sin (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.22">Da 4:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.30">30</reference>).<div eID="gen13982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13983" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the terrible--</hi>rather, tyrants [Horsley]. <div eID="gen13983" type="x-p"/>
entries.1af03e96766c233edbcc8991cf153c7ccc45868e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8559"/><div sID="gen13984" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8559"/><hi type="bold">12. man ... precious--</hi>I will so cut off Babylon's defenders, that a single man shall be as rare and precious as the finest gold. <div eID="gen13984" type="x-p"/>
entries.d00a72d1236a4133e1781bcc64b3c3f312e97bba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8560"/><div sID="gen13985" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8560"/>13. Image for mighty revolutions (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.19">Is 24:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.34.4">34:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.6">Ha 3:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hag.2.6">Hag 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.11">Re 20:11</reference>). <div eID="gen13985" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb229641e7bd90ebf59f54ce594796c774b18950: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8561"/><div sID="gen13986" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8561"/><hi type="bold">14. it--</hi>Babylon.<div eID="gen13986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13987" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">roe--</hi>gazelle; the most timid and easily startled.<div eID="gen13987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13988" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no man taketh up--</hi>sheep defenseless, without a shepherd (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.7">Zec 13:7</reference>).<div eID="gen13988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13989" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every man ... to his own people--</hi>The "mingled peoples" of foreign lands shall flee out of her (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.16">Jr 50:16</reference>, 28, 37; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.9">51:9</reference>). <div eID="gen13989" type="x-p"/>
entries.e8874e44425c50b589f87a28eeb06d2afb2b9a95: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8562"/><div sID="gen13990" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8562"/><hi type="bold">15. found--</hi>in the city.<div eID="gen13990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13991" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">joined--</hi>"intercepted" [Maurer]. "Every one that has withdrawn himself," namely, to hide in the houses [Gesenius]. <div eID="gen13991" type="x-p"/>
entries.2335cd872b52f5b449a88bd760b6adfe336672e4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8563"/><div sID="gen13992" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8563"/>16. (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.8">Psa 137:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.137.9">9</reference>). <div eID="gen13992" type="x-p"/>
entries.afc6a3ffba87b484abcc2eb53db957afe3508cf4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8564"/><div sID="gen13993" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8564"/><hi type="bold">17. Medes--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.21.2">Is 21:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.11">Jr 51:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.28">28</reference>). At that time they were subject to Assyria; subsequently Arbaces, satrap of Media, revolted against the effeminate Sardanapalus, king of Assyria, destroyed Nineveh, and became king of Media, in the ninth century B.C.<div eID="gen13993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13994" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not regard silver--</hi>In vain will one try to buy his life from them for a ransom. The heathen Xenophon (Cyropædia, 5,1,10) represents Cyrus as attributing this characteristic to the Medes, disregard of riches. A curious confirmation of this prophecy. <div eID="gen13994" type="x-p"/>
entries.59a9086e6f4d01544878b057e37c7c6d50aca2cf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8565"/><div sID="gen13995" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8565"/><hi type="bold">18. bows--</hi>in the use of which the Persians were particularly skilled. <div eID="gen13995" type="x-p"/>
entries.a050ab7a7c5694a7c4a9b05650f8eff355803c56: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8566"/><div sID="gen13996" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8566"/><hi type="bold">19. glory of kingdoms--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.14.4">Is 14:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.47.5">47:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.41">Jr 51:41</reference>).<div eID="gen13996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13997" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beauty of ... excellency--</hi>Hebrew, "the glory of the pride" of the Chaldees; it was their glory and boast.<div eID="gen13997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13998" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as ... Gomorrah--</hi>as utterly (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.18">Jr 49:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.40">50:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.4.11">Am 4:11</reference>). Taken by Cyrus, by clearing out the canal made for emptying the superfluous waters of the Euphrates, and directing the river into this new channel, so that he was able to enter the city by the old bed in the night. <div eID="gen13998" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d460e85fcf27bd59de0500f1cfae07f8c967569: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8567"/><div sID="gen13999" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8567"/>20. Literally fulfilled.<div eID="gen13999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14000" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither ... Arabian pitch tent--</hi>Not only shall it not be a permanent residence, but not even a temporary resting-place. The Arabs, through dread of evil spirits, and believing the ghost of Nimrod to haunt it, will not pass the night there (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.13.21">Is 13:21</reference>).<div eID="gen14000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14001" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither ... shepherds--</hi>The region was once most fertile; but owing to the Euphrates being now no longer kept within its former channels, it has become a stagnant marsh, unfit for flocks; and on the wastes of its ruins (bricks and cement) no grass grows. <div eID="gen14001" type="x-p"/>
entries.e7847ed9acb11f0b36b9f3c0d3d81fff0c8b6a90: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8568"/><div sID="gen14002" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8568"/><hi type="bold">21. wild beasts--</hi>Hebrew, tsiyim, animals dwelling in arid wastes. Wild cats, remarkable for their howl [Bochart].<div eID="gen14002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14003" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">doleful creatures--</hi>"howling beasts," literally, "howlings" [Maurer].<div eID="gen14003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14004" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">owls--</hi>rather, "ostriches"; a timorous creature, delighting in solitary deserts and making a hideous noise [Bochart].<div eID="gen14004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14005" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">satyrs--</hi>sylvan demi-gods--half man, half goat--believed by the Arabs to haunt these ruins; probably animals of the goat-ape species [Vitringa]. Devil-worshippers, who dance amid the ruins on a certain night [J. Wolff]. <div eID="gen14005" type="x-p"/>
entries.393ce7db70a1a57f608642d85fadf04d198a10e9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8569"/><div sID="gen14006" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8569"/><hi type="bold">22. wild beasts of the islands--</hi>rather, "jackals"; called by the Arabs "sons of howling"; an animal midway between a fox and a wolf [Bochart and Maurer].<div eID="gen14006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14007" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cry--</hi>rather, "answer," "respond" to each other, as wolves do at night, producing a most dismal effect.<div eID="gen14007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14008" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dragons--</hi>serpents of various species, which hiss and utter dolorous sounds. Fable gave them wings, because they stand with much of the body elevated and then dart swiftly. Maurer understands here another species of jackal.<div eID="gen14008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14009" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">her time ... near--</hi>though one hundred seventy-four years distant, yet "near" to Isaiah, who is supposed to be speaking to the Jews as if now captives in Babylon (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.1">Is 14:1</reference>, 2). <chapter eID="Isa.13"/>

entries.380c72412833c5b210c7d0ec97bcee8e4954e45d: <div eID="gen27053" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen27054" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27055" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27055" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27054" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27056" type="x-p"/> God mustereth the armies of his wrath against the inhabitants of Babylon, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.1-Isa.13.6">Isa 13:1-6</reference>. The dreadful consequences of this visitation, and the terror and dismay of those who are the objects of it, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.7-Isa.13.16">Isa 13:7-16</reference>. The horrid cruelties that shall be indicted upon the Babylonians by the Medes, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.17">Isa 13:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.18">Isa 13:18</reference>. Total and irrecoverable desolation of Babylon, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.19-Isa.13.22">Isa 13:19-22</reference>. <div eID="gen27056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27057" type="x-p"/> This and the following chapter, - striking off the five last verses of the latter, which belong to a quite different subject, - contain one entire prophecy, foretelling the destruction of Babylon by the Medes and Persians; delivered probably in the reign of Ahaz, (see Vitrinya, 1:380), about two hundred years before its accomplishment. The captivity itself of the Jews at Babylon, which the prophet does not expressly foretell, but supposes, in the spirit of prophecy, as what was actually to be effected, did not fully take place till about one hundred and thirty years after the delivery of this prophecy: and the Medes, who are expressly mentioned <reference osisRef="Isa.13.17">Isa 13:17</reference>, as the principal agents in the overthrow of the Babylonian monarchy, by which the Jews were released from that captivity, were at this time an inconsiderable people; having been in a state of anarchy ever since the fall of the great Assyrian empire, of which they had made a part, under Sardanapalus; and did not become a kingdom under Deioces till about the seventeenth of Hezekiah. <div eID="gen27057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27058" type="x-p"/> The former part of this prophecy is one of the most beautiful examples that can be given of elegance of composition, variety of imagery, and sublimity of sentiment and diction, in the prophetic style; and the latter part consists of an ode of supreme and singular excellence. <div eID="gen27058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27059" type="x-p"/> The prophecy opens with the command of God to gather together the forces which he had destined to this service, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.2">Isa 13:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.3">Isa 13:3</reference>. Upon which the prophet immediately hears the tumultuous noise of the different nations crowding together to his standard; he sees them advancing, prepared to execute the Divine wrath, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.4">Isa 13:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.5">Isa 13:5</reference>. He proceeds to describe the dreadful consequences of this visitation, the consternation which will seize those who are the objects of it; and, transferring unawares the speech from himself to God, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.11">Isa 13:11</reference>, sets forth, under a variety of the most striking images, the dreadful destruction of the inhabitants of Babylon which will follow, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.11-Isa.13.16">Isa 13:11-16</reference>, and the everlasting desolation to which that great city is doomed, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.17-Isa.13.22">Isa 13:17-22</reference>. <div eID="gen27059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27060" type="x-p"/> The deliverance of Judah from captivity, the immediate consequence of this great revolution, is then set forth, without being much enlarged upon, or greatly amplified, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.1">Isa 14:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.2">Isa 14:2</reference>. This introduces, with the greatest ease and the utmost propriety, the triumphant song on that subject, verses 4-28. The beauties of which, the various images, scenes, persons introduced, and the elegant transitions from one to another, I shall here endeavor to point out in their order, leaving a few remarks upon particular passages of these two chapters to be given after these general observations on the whole. <div eID="gen27060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27061" type="x-p"/> A chorus of Jews is introduced, expressing their surprise and astonishment at the sudden downfall of Babylon; and the great reverse of fortune that had befallen the tyrant, who, like his predecessors, had oppressed his own and harassed the neighboring kingdoms. These oppressed kingdoms, or their rulers, are represented under the image of the fir trees and the cedars of Libanus, frequently used to express any thing in the political or religious world that is super-eminently great and majestic: the whole earth shouteth for joy; the cedars of Libanus utter a severe taunt over the fallen tyrant, and boast their security now he is no more. <div eID="gen27061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27062" type="x-p"/> The scene is immediately changed, and a new set of persons is introduced. The regions of the dead are laid open, and Hades is represented as rousing up the shades of the departed monarchs: they rise from their thrones to meet the king of Babylon at his coming; and insult him on his being reduced to the same low estate of impotence and dissolution with themselves. This is one of the boldest prosopopoeias that ever was attempted in poetry; and is executed with astonishing brevity and perspicuity, and with that peculiar force which in a great subject naturally results from both. The image of the state of the dead, or the infernum poeticum of the Hebrews, is taken from their custom of burying, those at least of the higher rank, in large sepulchral vaults hewn in the rock. Of this kind of sepulchres there are remains at Jerusalem now extant; and some that are said to be the sepulchres of the kings of Judah. See Maundrell, p. 76. You are to form to yourself an idea of an immense subterranean vault, a vast gloomy cavern, all round the sides of which there are cells to receive the dead bodies; here the deceased monarchs lie in a distinguished sort of state, suitable to their former rank, each on his own couch, with his arms beside him, his sword at his head, and the bodies of his chiefs and companions round about him. See <reference osisRef="Eze.32.27">Eze 32:27</reference>. On which place Sir John Chardin's MS. note is as follows: "En Mingrelie ils dorment tous leurs epees sous leurs tetes, et leurs autres armes a leur cote; et on les enterre de mesme, leurs armes poseess de cette facon." In Mingrelia they always sleep with their swords under their heads, and their other arms by their sides; and they bury their dead with their arms placed in the same manner. These illustrious shades rise at once from their couches, as from their thrones; and advance to the entrance of the cavern to meet the king of Babylon, and to receive him with insults on his fall. <div eID="gen27062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27063" type="x-p"/> The Jews now resume the speech; they address the king of Babylon as the morning-star fallen from heaven, as the first in splendor and dignity in the political world, fallen from his high state; they introduce him as uttering the most extravagant vaunts of his power and ambitious designs in his former glory. These are strongly contrasted in the close with his present low and abject condition. <div eID="gen27063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27064" type="x-p"/> Immediately follows a different scene, and a most happy image, to diversify the same subject, to give it a new turn, and an additional force. Certain persons are introduced who light upon the corpse of the king of Babylon, cast out and lying naked on the bare ground, among the common slain, just after the taking of the city; covered with wounds, and so disfigured, that it is some time before they know him. They accost him with the severest taunts; and bitterly reproach him with his destructive ambition, and his cruel usage of the conquered; which have deservedly brought him this ignominious treatment, so different from that which those of his rank usually meet with, and which shall cover his posterity with disgrace. <div eID="gen27064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27065" type="x-p"/> To complete the whole, God is introduced, declaring the fate of Babylon, the utter extirpation of the royal family, and the total desolation of the city; the deliverance of his people, and the destruction of their enemies; confirming the irreversible decree by the awful sanction of his oath. <div eID="gen27065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27066" type="x-p"/> I believe it may with truth be affirmed, that there is no poem of its kind extant in any language, in which the subject is so well laid out, and 60 happily conducted, with such a richness of invention, with such variety of images, persons, and distinct actions, with such rapidity and ease of transition, in so small a compass, as in this ode of Isaiah. For beauty of disposition, strength of colouring, greatness of sentiment, brevity, perspicuity, and force of expression, it stands, among all the monuments of antiquity, unrivalled. - L. <div eID="gen27066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27067" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen27067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27068" type="x-p"/> The burden of Babylon - The prophecy that foretells its destruction by the Medes and Persians: see the preceding observations.
entries.ffa9bec5d837350faddc2f0f65e98e85777259aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen27068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27069" type="x-p"/> Exalt the voice - The word להם lahem, "to them," which is of no use, and rather weakens the sentence, is omitted by an ancient MS., and the Vulgate.
entries.272e95f2dbeb8cdfc5ea11951514afdfc22ae6b1: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen27069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27070" type="x-p"/> I have commanded my sanctified ones - מקדשי mekuddashai, the persons consecrated to this very purpose. Nothing can be plainer than that the verb כדש kadash, "to make holy," signifies also to consecrate or appoint to a particular purpose. Bishop Lowth translates, "my enrolled warriors." This is the sense.
entries.dcd14e70c56434fcd00fab0fd36c699f5cab3e03: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen27070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27071" type="x-p"/> Of the battle "For the battle" - The Bodleian MS. has למלחמה lemilchamah. Cyrus's army was made up of many different nations. Jeremiah calls it an "assembly of great nations from the north country," <reference osisRef="Jer.50.9">Jer 50:9</reference>. And afterwards mentions the kingdoms of "Ararat, Minni, and Ashchenaz, (i.e. Armenia, Corduene, Pontus or Phrygia, Vitring.), with the kings of the Medes," <reference osisRef="Jer.51.27">Jer 51:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.28">Jer 51:28</reference>. See Xenophon. Cyrop.
entries.b4c27a834e1c7092d517ac2782d13c023f878d3f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen27071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27072" type="x-p"/> They come from a far country - The word מארץ meerets is wanting in one MS. and in the Syriac: "They come from afar." <div eID="gen27072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27073" type="x-p"/> From the end of heaven - Kimchi says, Media, "the end of heaven," in Scripture phrase, means, the East.
entries.2f755fdb92f23bdd664b377858ca1a4435c9eeeb: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen27073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27074" type="x-p"/> And they shall be afraid "And they shall be terrified" - I join this verb, ונבהלו venibhalu, to the preceding verse, with the Syriac and Vulgate. <div eID="gen27074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27075" type="x-p"/> Pangs and sorrows shall take hold on them "Pangs shall seize them" - The Septuagint, Syriac, and Chaldee read יאחזום yochezum, instead of יאחזון yochezun, which does not express the pronoun then, necessary to the sense.
entries.d7dd25be33a442924fe4c9cba299f5bda6de8a74: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen27075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27076" type="x-p"/> For the stars of heaven "Yea, the stars of heaven" - The Hebrew poets, to express happiness, prosperity, the instauration and advancement of states, kingdoms, and potentates, make use of images taken from the most striking parts of nature, from the heavenly bodies, from the sun, moon, and stars: which they describe as shining with increased splendor, and never setting. The moon becomes like the meridian sun, and the sun's light is augmented sevenfold; (see <reference osisRef="Isa.30.26">Isa 30:26</reference>); new heavens and a new earth are created, and a brighter age commences. On the contrary, the overflow and destruction of kingdoms is represented by opposite images. The stars are obscured, the moon withdraws her light, and the sun shines no more! The earth quakes, and the heavens tremble; and all things seem tending to their original chaos, See <reference osisRef="Joe.2.10">Joe 2:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joe.3.15">Joe 3:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joe.3.16">Joe 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amo.8.9">Amo 8:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mat.24.29">Mat 24:29</reference>; and De S. Poes. Herb. Prael. 6 et IX. <div eID="gen27076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27077" type="x-p"/> And the moon shall not cause her light to shine - This in its farther reference may belong to the Jewish polity, both in Church and state, which should be totally eclipsed, and perhaps shine no more in its distinct state for ever.
entries.56c46ae6517eefa28783358c37ba15b26333a74b: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen27077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27078" type="x-p"/> I will punish the world "I will visit the world" - That is, the Babylonish empire; as η οικουμενη, for the Roman empire, or for Judea, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.1">Luk 2:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Act.11.28">Act 11:28</reference>. So the universus orbis Romanus, for the Roman empire; Salvian. lib. 5 Minos calls Crete his world: "Creten, quae meus est orbis," Ovid. Metamorph. 8:9.
entries.73b01e54204f4b570671617e6f16a08b56b28952: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen27078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27079" type="x-p"/> I will make a man more precious than fine gold-wedge of Ophir - The Medes and Persians will not be satisfied with the spoils of the Babylonians. They seek either to destroy or enslave them; and they will accept no ransom for any man - either for אנוש enosh, the poor man, or for אדם adam, the more honorable person. All must fall by the sword, or go into captivity together; for the Medes, (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.17">Isa 13:17</reference>), regard not silver, and delight not in gold.
entries.282be8ab47bec3978c8d41185bb2413f54d992de: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> "And the remnant" - Here is plainly a defect in this sentence, as it stands in the Hebrew text; the subject of the proposition is lost. What is it that shall be like a roe chased? The Septuagint happily supply it, οἱ καταλελειμμενοι, שאר shear, the remnant. A MS. here supplies the word יושב yosheb, the inhabitant; which makes a tolerably good sense; but I much prefer the reading of the Septuagint. <div eID="gen27079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27080" type="x-p"/> They shall - turn "They shall look" - That is, the forces of the king of Babylon, destitute of their leader, and all his auxiliaries, collected from Asia Minor, and other distant countries, shall disperse and flee to their respective homes.
entries.924420f4c17f9bcce025eafb073d3b07ca37eb8a: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen27080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27081" type="x-p"/> Every one that is found "Every one that is overtaken" - That is, none shall escape from the slaughter; neither they who flee singly, dispersed and in confusion; nor they who endeavor to make their retreat in a more regular manner, by forming compact bodies: they shall all be equally cut off by the sword of the enemy. The Septuagint have understood it in this sense, which they have well expressed: - Ὁς γαρ αν ἁλῳ ἡττηθησεται, Και οἱτινες συνηγμενοι εισι πεσουνται μαχαιρα. "Whosoever is caught shall be overthrown, <div eID="gen27081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27082" type="x-p"/> And all that are collected together shall fall by the sword." <div eID="gen27082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27083" type="x-p"/> Where, for ἡττηθησεται, MS. Pachom has εκκενθησεται, et οἱ Γ Cod. Marchal. in margine, et MS. 1. D. 2: εκκεντηθησεται, which seems to be right, being properly expressive of the Hebrew.
entries.19a550876266bffdb9ad8f21443c2a381d06da42: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen27083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27084" type="x-p"/> Which shall not regard silver "Who shall hold silver of no account" - That is, who shall not be induced, by large offers of gold and silver for ransom, to spare the lives of those whom they have subdued in battle; their rage and cruelty will get the better of all such motives. We have many examples in the Iliad and in the Aeneid of addresses of the vanquished to the pity and avarice of the vanquishers, to induce them to spare their lives. <div eID="gen27084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27085" type="x-p"/> Est domus alta: jacent penitus defossa talenta <div eID="gen27085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27086" type="x-p"/> Caelati argenti: sunt auri ponders facti <div eID="gen27086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27087" type="x-p"/> Infectique mihi: non hic victoria Teucrum <div eID="gen27087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27088" type="x-p"/> Vertitur; aut anima una dalbit discrimina tanta. <div eID="gen27088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27089" type="x-p"/> Dixerat: Aeneas contra cui talia reddit: <div eID="gen27089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27090" type="x-p"/> Argenti atque auri memoras quae multa talenta <div eID="gen27090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27091" type="x-p"/> Gnatis parce tuis. <div eID="gen27091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27092" type="x-p"/> Aen. 10:526. "High in my dome are silver talents rolled, <div eID="gen27092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27093" type="x-p"/> With piles of labored and unlaboured gold. <div eID="gen27093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27094" type="x-p"/> These, to procure my ransom, I resign; <div eID="gen27094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27095" type="x-p"/> The war depends not on a life like mine: <div eID="gen27095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27096" type="x-p"/> One, one poor life can no such difference yield, <div eID="gen27096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27097" type="x-p"/> Nor turn the mighty balance of the field. <div eID="gen27097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27098" type="x-p"/> Thy talents, (cried the prince), thy treasured store <div eID="gen27098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27099" type="x-p"/> Keep for thy sons." <div eID="gen27099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27100" type="x-p"/> Pitt. <div eID="gen27100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27101" type="x-p"/> It is remarkable that Xenophon makes Cyrus open a speech to his army, and in particular to the Medes, who made the principal part of it, with praising them for their disregard of riches. Ανδρες Μηδοι, και παντες οἱ παροντες, εγω ὑμας οιδα σαφως, ὁτι ουτε χρηματων δεομενοι συν εμοι εξελθετε· "Ye Medes, and others who now hear me, I well know that you have not accompanied me in this expedition with a view of acquiring wealth." - Cyrop. lib. v.
entries.b055c557743a92c0c429ba771ae45e166c632994: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen27101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27102" type="x-p"/> Their bows also shall dash "Their bows shall dash" - Both Herodotus, 1:61, and Xenophon, Anab. iii., mention, that the Persians used large bows τοξα μεγαλα: and the latter says particularly that their bows were three cubits long, Anab. 4. They were celebrated for their archers, see <reference osisRef="Isa.22.6">Isa 22:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.35">Jer 49:35</reference>. Probably their neighbours and allies, the Medes, dealt much in the same sort of arms. In <reference osisRef="Psa.18.34">Psa 18:34</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Job.20.24">Job 20:24</reference>, mention is made of a bow of steel; if the Persian bows were of metal, we may easily conceive that with a metalline bow of three cubits' length, and proportionably strong, the soldiers might dash and slay the young men, the weaker and unresisting of the inhabitants (for they are joined with the fruit of the womb and the children) in the general carnage on taking the city. תרתשנה terattashnah, shall be broken or shivered to pieces. This seems to refer, not to נערים nearim, young men, but to קשתות keshathoth, their bows. The bows of the young men shall be broken to pieces. <div eID="gen27102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27103" type="x-p"/> On the fruit, etc. "And on the fruit," etc. - A MS. of Dr. Kennicott's reads ועל פרי veal peri and on the fruit. And nine MSS. (three ancient) and two editions, with the Septuagint, Vulgate, and Syriac, add likewise the conjunction ו vau, and, to על al, upon, afterwards.
entries.923cc3e271f49594845d59239f7b34dc92ae76c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen27103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27104" type="x-p"/> And Babylon - The great city of Babylon was at this time rising to its height of glory, while the Prophet Isaiah was repeatedly denouncing its utter destruction. From the first of Hezekiah to the first of Nebuchadnezzar, under whom it was brought to the highest degree of strength and splendor, are about one hundred and twenty years. I will here very briefly mention some particulars of the greatness of the place, and note the several steps by which this remarkable prophecy was at length accomplished in the total ruin of it. <div eID="gen27104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27105" type="x-p"/> It was, according to the lowest account given of it by ancient historians, a regular square, forty-five miles in compass, inclosed by a wall two hundred feet high and fifty broad; in which there were a hundred gates of brass. Its principal ornaments were the temple of Belus, in the middle of which was a tower of eight stories of building, upon a base of a quarter of a mile square, a most magnificent palace, and the famous hanging gardens, which were an artificial mountain, raised upon arches, and planted with trees of the largest as well as the most beautiful sorts. <div eID="gen27105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27106" type="x-p"/> Cyrus took the city by diverting the waters of the Euphrates which ran through the midst of it, and entering the place at night by the dry channel. The river being never restored afterward to its proper course, overflowed the whole country, and made it little better than a great morass; this and the great slaughter of the inhabitants, with other bad consequences of the taking of the city, was the first step to the ruin of the place. The Persian monarchs ever regarded it with a jealous eye; they kept it under, and took care to prevent its recovering its former greatness. Darius Hystaspes not long afterward most severely punished it for a revolt, greatly depopulated the place, lowered the walls, and demolished the gates. Xerxes destroyed the temples, and with the rest the great temple of Belus, Herod. 3:159, Arrian Exp. Alexandri, lib. 7. The building of Seleucia on the Tigris exhausted Babylon by its neighborhood, as well as by the immediate loss of inhabitants taken away by Seleucus to people his new city, Strabo, lib. 16. A king of the Parthians soon after carried away into slavery a great number of the inhabitants, and burned and destroyed the most beautiful parts of the city, Valesii Excerpt. Diodori, p. 377. Strabo (ibid.) says that in his time great part of it was a mere desert; that the Persians had partly destroyed it; and that time and the neglect of the Macedonians, while they were masters of it, had nearly completed its destruction. Jerome (in loc.) says that in his time it was quite in ruins, and that the walls served only for the inclosure for a park or forest for the king's hunting. Modern travelers, who have endeavored to find the remains of it, have given but a very unsatisfactory account of their success. What Benjamin of Tudela and Pietro della Valle supposed to have been some of its ruins, Tavernier thinks are the remains of some late Arabian building. Upon the whole, Babylon is so utterly annihilated, that even the place where this wonder of the world stood cannot now be determined with any certainty! See also note on <reference osisRef="Isa.43.14">Isa 43:14</reference> (note). <div eID="gen27106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27107" type="x-p"/> We are astonished at the accounts which ancient historians of the best credit give of the immense extent, height, and thickness of the walls of Nineveh and Babylon; nor are we less astonished when we are assured, by the concurrent testimony of modern travelers, that no remains, not the least traces, of these prodigious works are now to be found. Scattered fragments of its tiles and bricks are yet to be found. Proud Babylon reduced now to a few brick-bats! Our wonder will, I think, be moderated in both respects, if we consider the fabric of these celebrated walls, and the nature of the materials of which they consisted. Buildings in the east have always been, and are to this day, made of earth or clay, mixed or beat up with straw to make the parts cohere, and dried only in the sun. This is their method of making bricks; see on <reference osisRef="Isa.9.9">Isa 9:9</reference> (note). The walls of the city were built of the earth digged out on the spot, and dried upon the place, by which means both the ditch and the wall were at once formed, the former furnishing materials for the latter. That the walls of Babylon were of this kind is well known; and Berosus expressly says, (apud Joseph. Antiq. 10:11), that Nebuchadnezzar added three new walls both to the old and new city, partly of brick and bitumen, and partly of brick alone. A wall of this sort must have a great thickness in proportion to its height, otherwise it cannot stand. The thickness of the walls of Babylon is said to have been one-fourth of their height, which seems to have been no more than was absolutely necessary. Maundrell, speaking of the garden walls of Damascus, says, "They are of a very singular structure. They are built of great pieces of earth, made in the fashion of brick, and hardened in the sun. In their dimensions they are two yards long each, and somewhat more than one broad, and half a yard thick." And afterward, speaking of the walls of the houses, he says, "From this dirty way of building they have this amongst other inconveniences, that upon any violent rain the whole city becomes, by the washing of the houses, as it were a quagmire," p. 124. And see note on <reference osisRef="Isa.30.13">Isa 30:13</reference>. When a wall of this sort comes to be out of repair, and is neglected, it is easy to conceive the necessary consequences, namely, that in no long course of ages it must be totally destroyed by the heavy rains, and at length washed away, and reduced to its original earth. - L.
entries.3f9b32edbab1265400630b456d9649964ac01396: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen27107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27108" type="x-p"/> Satyrs - A kind of beast like to man, which is called מרמוטש marmots, a monkey. - Rabbi Parchon.
entries.4f4cebbec5b553724baf5fd1112bb4a857a19887: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen27108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27109" type="x-p"/> In their pleasant palaces "In their palaces" - באלמנותיו bealmenothaiv; a plain mistake, I presume, for בארמנתיו bearmenothaiv. It is so corrected in two MSS., the Syriac, Chaldee, and Vulgate. Πουλυποδες δ' εν εμοι θαλαμας φωκαι τε μελαιναι Οικα ποιησονται ακηδεα, χητεΐ λαων. <div eID="gen27109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27110" type="x-p"/> Hom.
